claim: Plant meristems carry pools of continuously active stem cells.
source: Plant meristems carry pools of continuously active stem cells, whose activity is controlled by developmental and environmental signals.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in plant biology.

claim: Stem cell activity in plant meristems is controlled by developmental and environmental signals.
source: Plant meristems carry pools of continuously active stem cells, whose activity is controlled by developmental and environmental signals.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in plant biology.

claim: After stem cell division, daughter cells that exit the stem cell domain acquire transit amplifying cell identity before they are incorporated into organs and differentiate.
source: After stem cell division, daughter cells that exit the stem cell domain acquire transit amplifying cell identity before they are incorporated into organs and differentiate.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the developmental trajectory of stem cells.

claim: HEC function stabilizes cell fate in distinct zones of the shoot meristem.
source: Our work reveals that HEC function stabilizes cell fate in distinct zones of the shoot meristem thereby controlling the spatio-temporal dynamics of stem cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: HEC function controls the spatio-temporal dynamics of stem cell differentiation.
source: Our work reveals that HEC function stabilizes cell fate in distinct zones of the shoot meristem thereby controlling the spatio-temporal dynamics of stem cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: HEC activity is concomitant with the local modulation of cellular responses to cytokinin and auxin.
source: Importantly, this activity is concomitant with the local modulation of cellular responses to cytokinin and auxin, two key phytohormones regulating cell behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by reporter analysis and experimental data.

claim: HEC factors transcriptionally control MONOPTEROS (MP).
source: Mechanistically, we show that HEC factors transcriptionally control and physically interact with MONOPTEROS (MP), a key regulator of auxin signalling, and modulate the autocatalytic stabilization of auxin signalling output.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract, supported by RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: HEC factors physically interact with MONOPTEROS (MP).
source: Mechanistically, we show that HEC factors transcriptionally control and physically interact with MONOPTEROS (MP), a key regulator of auxin signalling, and modulate the autocatalytic stabilization of auxin signalling output.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract, supported by Yeast-2-Hybrid and BiFC assays.

claim: HEC factors modulate the autocatalytic stabilization of auxin signalling output.
source: Mechanistically, we show that HEC factors transcriptionally control and physically interact with MONOPTEROS (MP), a key regulator of auxin signalling, and modulate the autocatalytic stabilization of auxin signalling output.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data showing effects on auxin feedback.

claim: Plants employ a postembryonic mode of development based on the continuous activity of pluripotent stem cells embedded in specialized tissues called meristems.
source: Firstly, plants employ a postembryonic mode of development, which is based on the continuous activity of pluripotent stem cells embedded in specialized tissues, called meristems.
evidence: This is established knowledge in plant developmental biology.

claim: Plant development is modular and the same set of organs is initiated repeatedly from a stem cell system.
source: Secondly, plant development is modular and thus the same set of organs is initiated repeatedly from a stem cell system, greatly facilitating in vivo analysis of cell-decision-making.
evidence: This is established knowledge in plant developmental biology.

claim: Plant cell identity is determined by position rather than lineage due to the encasement by a cell wall.
source: Thirdly, due to the encasement by a cell wall, plant cells are immobile and thus their identity is determined by position, rather than lineage and can change multiple times during their development until terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in plant developmental biology.

claim: In the shoot apical meristem (SAM), two major fate transitions can be identified: from stem cells in the central zone (CZ) to transit amplifying cells in the peripheral zone (PZ) and further on into organ primordia.
source: In the shoot apical meristem (SAM), the stem cell system responsible for the generation of all above ground structures, two major fate transitions can be identified: From stem cells in the central zone (CZ) to transit amplifying cells in the peripheral zone (PZ) and further on into organ primordia, which will give rise to fully differentiated lateral structures, such as leaves or flowers (reviewed in [Gaillochet et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is established knowledge in plant developmental biology, supported by a citation.

claim: Cell fate trajectories in the SAM are instructed by an intertwined communication system between local transcriptional networks and non-cell autonomous phytohormone signals.
source: At the molecular level, cell fate trajectories are instructed by an intertwined communication system between local transcriptional networks and non-cell autonomous phytohormone signals (Brand et al., 2000; Gordon et al., 2009; Jasinski et al., 2005; Leibfried et al., 2005; Schoof et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Stem cell fate in the SAM is dependent on the homeodomain transcription factor WUSCHEL (WUS).
source: Stem cell fate in the SAM is dependent on the homeodomain transcription factor WUSCHEL (WUS), whose RNA is expressed in the organising centre (OC), located below the stem cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: WUS protein moves apically through plasmodesmata into the overlying cells where it is required to maintain stem cell identity.
source: WUS protein moves apically through plasmodesmata into the overlying cells, where it is required to maintain stem cell identity (Daum et al., 2014; Yadav et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Stem cells in the SAM express CLAVATA3 (CLV3), a short, secreted peptide that acts to limit WUS expression.
source: Stem cells in turn express CLAVATA3 (CLV3), a short, secreted peptide that acts to limit WUS expression via the CLV1, CLV2, CORYNE (CRN), BARELY ANY MERISTEM (BAM) receptors system (Bleckmann et al., 2010; Clark et al., 1997; Fletcher et al., 1999; Nimchuk et al., 2015; Ohyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The WUS/CLV3 negative feedback loop represents the core module of SAM regulation and couples the size of the OC with that of the CZ.
source: The resulting negative feedback loop represents the core module of SAM regulation and couples the size of the OC with that of the CZ (Brand et al., 2000; Schoof et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM) is required throughout the SAM to inhibit differentiation by stimulation of cytokinin production and repression of gibberellic acid (GA) biosynthesis.
source: In parallel, the KNOTTED-like homeobox transcription factor SHOOT MERISTEMLESS (STM) is required throughout the SAM to inhibit differentiation by stimulation of cytokinin production and repression of gibberellic acid (GA) biosynthesis (Jasinski et al., 2005; Long et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: WUS represses A-Type ARABIDOPSIS RESPONSE REGULATOR (ARR) genes in the centre of the SAM.
source: In the centre of the SAM, WUS represses A-Type ARABIDOPSIS RESPONSE REGULATOR (ARR) genes, which encode for negative feedback factors in cytokinin signalling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: WUS acts to sensitize the cellular environment to cytokinin, which in turn promotes WUS expression, creating a positive feedback loop.
source: In essence, WUS acts to sensitize the cellular environment to cytokinin, which in turn promotes WUS expression thus creating a positive feedback loop that helps to establish and maintain the OC (Gordon et al., 2009; Leibfried et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cytokinin plays a key role in controlling cell proliferation in the SAM by stimulating CYCLIN D3 expression.
source: Cytokinin also plays a key role in controlling cell proliferation in the SAM by stimulating CYCLIN D3 expression (Riou-Khamlichi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: WUS directly represses the expression of HECATE1 (HEC1).
source: In addition to its role in integrating hormonal signals, WUS directly represses the expression of HECATE1 (HEC1), which encodes a bHLH transcription factor that redundantly functions with its closest paralogs HEC2 and HEC3 in various developmental contexts (Gremski et al., 2007; Schuster et al., 2015; Schuster et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HEC1 mRNA is expressed throughout the SAM but excluded from the OC.
source: In line with this regulation, HEC1 mRNA is expressed throughout the SAM, but excluded from the OC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Schuster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: HEC1 protein displays limited intercellular movement.
source: This pattern is faithfully translated into protein accumulation, since HEC1 protein displays limited intercellular movement (Daum et al., 2014; Schuster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Uncoupling HEC1 expression from WUS in the OC leads to SAM termination.
source: Importantly, the precise spatial control of HEC1 activity by WUS is essential for SAM function, since uncoupling HEC1 expression from WUS in the OC leads to SAM termination, whereas enhancing HEC1 activity in stem cells leads to massive over-accumulation of these cells followed by a progressive repression of the core WUS/CLV3 feedback system (Schuster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Enhancing HEC1 activity in stem cells leads to massive over-accumulation of these cells followed by a progressive repression of the core WUS/CLV3 feedback system.
source: Importantly, the precise spatial control of HEC1 activity by WUS is essential for SAM function, since uncoupling HEC1 expression from WUS in the OC leads to SAM termination, whereas enhancing HEC1 activity in stem cells leads to massive over-accumulation of these cells followed by a progressive repression of the core WUS/CLV3 feedback system (Schuster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: HEC function is mediated by the formation of a protein complex between HEC and the bHLH transcription factor SPATULA (SPT).
source: Mechanistically, this function is mediated by the formation of a protein complex between HEC and the bHLH transcription factor SPATULA (SPT) (Schuster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Local auxin signalling maxima are dynamically formed through a combination of auxin biosynthesis and the controlled intracellular polarization of the auxin transporter PIN-FORMED1 (PIN1) by the activity of the protein kinase PINOID (PID).
source: Local auxin signalling maxima are dynamically formed through a combination of different mechanisms that include auxin biosynthesis and the controlled intracellular polarization of the auxin transporter PIN-FORMED1 (PIN1) by the activity of the protein kinase PINOID (PID) (Benjamins et al., 2001; Pinon et al., 2013; Reinhardt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dynamic auxin maxima are translated into robust auxin signalling output by AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR transcription factors, such as ARF5/MONOPTEROS (ARF5/MP).
source: Dynamic auxin maxima are translated into robust auxin signalling output by AUXIN RESPONSE FACTOR transcription factors, such as ARF5/MONOPTEROS (ARF5/MP) (Bhatia et al., 2016; Hardtke and Berleth, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MP associates with the chromatin remodelling factors SPLAYED (SYD) and BRAHMA (BRM), forming a regulatory protein complex sufficient to promote floral fate over undifferentiated SAM fate.
source: MP associates with the chromatin remodelling factors SPLAYED (SYD) and BRAHMA (BRM), forming a regulatory protein complex sufficient to promote floral fate over undifferentiated SAM fate (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The boundary zone (BZ) is required for proper spatial separation of organs from the SAM.
source: In addition to primordia initiation, a boundary zone (BZ), which surrounds the entire SAM like a ring is required for proper spatial separation of organs from the SAM (reviewed in [Žádníková and Simon, 2014]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The BZ is dependent on the activity of the CUP SHAPED COTYLEDONS (CUC) and LATERAL ORGANFUSION (LOF) genes.
source: The BZ is dependent on the activity of the CUP SHAPED COTYLEDONS (CUC) and LATERAL ORGANFUSION (LOF) genes and loss of their function results in extensive fusions of lateral organs with the active SAM (Aida et al., 1999; Gaillochet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MP relays auxin signals to the core WUS/CLV3 feedback loop by negatively regulating ARR7.
source: First, MP relays auxin signals to the core WUS/CLV3 feedback loop by negatively regulating ARR7 (Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Organ primordia produce the short peptide CLE27, which signals in the centre of the SAM through AtFEA3 and represses WUS expression.
source: Second, organ primordia produce the short peptide CLE27, which signals in the centre of the SAM through AtFEA3 and represses WUS expression (Je et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The rate of lateral organ initiation correlates with the size of the SAM and larger SAMs tend to produce more organs per unit of time.
source: As a consequence of these multiple regulatory loops, the rate of lateral organ initiation correlates with the size of the SAM and larger SAMs tend to produce more organs per unit of time (Landrein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: SAMs of hec1,2,3 triple mutants are smaller and display a reduced cell number.
source: When we applied this tool to plants that lack HEC function (hec1,2,3 triple mutants), we found that their SAMs were smaller and displayed a reduced cell number, in line with our previous results (Figure 1A–D) (Schuster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-D and a citation to previous work.

claim: Average cell size was not affected in SAMs of hec1,2,3 triple mutants.
source: Average cell size was not affected in SAMs of hec1,2,3 triple mutants, supporting that reduction in meristem size results from decreased cell number (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The average time interval between the initiation of successive lateral organs along the stem (plastochron) was substantially reduced in hec1,2,3 plants.
source: Surprisingly, the average time interval between the initiation of successive lateral organs along the stem (plastochron) was substantially reduced in hec1,2,3 plants, despite the smaller SAM (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Dex treatment of pCLV3:HEC1-linker-GR plants caused a gradual enlargement of the SAM over time.
source: In contrast to the mock control, dex treatment caused a gradual enlargement of the SAM over time, which was in line with our observation of constitutive pCLV3:HEC1-linker-GFP lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The increase in SAM size caused by stem cell-specific activation of HEC1 was accompanied by a transient enlargement of both the niche (OC) and the CZ.
source: Interestingly, the increase in SAM size caused by stem cell-specific activation of HEC1 was accompanied by a transient enlargement of both the niche, or organising centre (OC), and the CZ (Figure 2A–G; Figure 2—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-G and Figure 2—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: After an initial expansion of expression domains, the intensities of WUS and CLV3 reporters were strongly reduced at day 4.
source: After an initial expansion of expression domains, we found that the intensities of WUS and CLV3 reporters were strongly reduced at day 4, likely as an effect of a feedback mechanism restricting CZ and OC fate (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: HEC1 promotes SAM fasciation via transient stimulation of WUS.
source: This indirect negative effect of HEC1 on WUS and CLV3 expression explained our previous findings using stably expressing transgenes, which had shown a reduction in WUS and CLV3 expression (Schuster et al., 2014) and revealed that HEC1 promotes SAM fasciation via transient stimulation of WUS (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4B, and a citation.

claim: Cell division activity after stem cell specific induction of HEC1 was decreased at the centre of the SAM and mostly confined to the PZ.
source: Interestingly, we observed that although the SAM expanded, cell division activity after stem cell specific induction of HEC1 was decreased at the centre of the SAM and mostly confined to the PZ as in mock-treated plants (Figure 2I–L; Figure 2—figure supplement 6; Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2I-L and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: HEC1 did not locally promote stem cell division.
source: This demonstrated that HEC1 did not locally promote stem cell division.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell division activity data.

claim: Cell proliferation in the periphery was stimulated non-cell autonomously after stem cell specific induction of HEC1.
source: In contrast, we observed an increase in the mitotic index of the PZ at later stages (day 3 and day 4) despite the fact that HEC1 protein is largely unable to move from cell to cell, suggesting that cell proliferation in the periphery was stimulated non-cell autonomously (Figure 2L; Figure 2—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 6C, and inferred from the limited mobility of HEC1 protein.

claim: The ratio between CLV3 positive cells and all SAM cells remained essentially unchanged after stem cell specific expression of HEC1.
source: Interestingly, although the number of CLV3 positive cells strongly increased after dex treatment, the ratio between CLV3 and all SAM cells remained essentially unchanged (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: HEC1 activity locally inhibits the transition from stem cell to PZ fate.
source: Taken together, these two lines of experiments excluded that cell proliferation in the CZ or re-specification of early PZ cells were the main drivers of HEC1-mediated meristem expansion and left us with a model in which HEC1 activity would locally inhibit the transition from stem cell to PZ fate, giving rise to a larger stem cell domain and consequently to an enlarged shoot meristem.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of experimental data.

claim: HEC1 induction at the periphery and BZ gradually suppressed the emergence of lateral organs, eventually resulting in the formation of pin-like inflorescences.
source: Strikingly, HEC1 induction at the periphery and BZ gradually supressed the emergence of lateral organs, eventually resulting in the formation of pin-like inflorescences, demonstrating that HEC1 can potently interfere with incorporation of cells into organs when expressed at the BZ (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The developmental phenotypes observed in distinct domains of the SAM after HEC1 induction were fully suppressed in the spt mutant background.
source: Strikingly, the developmental phenotypes observed in distinct domains of the SAM were fully suppressed in the spt mutant background, including the formation of pin-like inflorescences after activation of HEC1 at the periphery (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: HEC genes are able to control CZ to PZ as well as PZ to organ primordia cell fate transitions.
source: Taken together, HEC function appeared not only to control stem cell to PZ, but also to be required and sufficient for PZ to organ fate transitions together with its partner SPT and thus acted as a central gatekeeper for cell fate progression throughout the SAM.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Combining an increased CZ to PZ transition with an increased primordia initiation rate in simulations could reproduce experimental measurements for the number of CZ cells, SAM cells and for the cumulated number of lateral organs.
source: By combining an increased CZ to PZ transition with an increased primordia initiation rate, our simulations could reproduce experimental measurements for the number of CZ cells, SAM cells and for the cumulated number of lateral organs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In hec1,2,3, primordia were initiated at a 15% higher rate and separated 10 hr earlier from the SAM than in wild type.
source: Importantly, our simulations not only qualitatively captured the dynamics of HEC loss-of-function meristem but also allowed us to compute that in hec1,2,3, primordia were initiated at a 15% higher rate and separated 10 hr earlier from the SAM than in wild type, supporting the idea that HEC function modulates the dynamics of stem cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a quantitative prediction from computational modeling.

claim: hec1,2,3 triple mutants displayed a substantial reduction in pTCSn:erGFP signal specific to the SAM.
source: In contrast to WT, hec1,2,3 triple mutants displayed a substantial reduction in pTCSn:erGFP signal specific to the SAM, whereas TCS activity in the root was unchanged (Figure 5A–C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Increased HEC1 activity in stem cells led to a significant expansion of the central cytokinin-signalling domain.
source: Conversely, increased HEC1 activity in stem cells led to a significant expansion of the central cytokinin-signalling domain, which was concomitant with SAM enlargement (Figure 5D–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Induction of HEC1 at the PZ and BZ did not locally promote cytokinin signalling.
source: Induction of HEC1 at the PZ and BZ did not locally promote cytokinin signalling, highlighting the domain-specific activity of HEC factors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Both chemical and genetic stimulation of cytokinin signalling largely suppressed SAM size defects of hec1,2,3 SAMs.
source: In our growth conditions, both chemical and genetic stimulation largely suppressed SAM size defects of hec1,2,3 SAMs (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: HEC function is sufficient and required to promote cytokinin signalling, which subsequently affects SAM size.
source: Together, these results showed that HEC function was sufficient and required to promote cytokinin signalling, which subsequently affected SAM size.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: The topology of auxin signalling input and output in the SAM was only mildly changed in hec1,2,3 compared to WT.
source: Our analysis showed that the topology of auxin signalling input and output in the SAM was only mildly changed in hec1,2,3 compared to WT (Figure 4E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that auxin signalling does not critically depend on HEC function.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Boosting HEC activity at the periphery led to a substantial reduction in the number of DR5 signal maxima.
source: Consistent with the increase in auxin output observed in hec1,2,3 mutants, boosting HEC activity at the periphery led to a substantial reduction in the number of DR5 signal maxima, eventually bringing about a complete collapse of lateral organ initiation (Figure 6A–C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Inducing HEC1 in stem cells repressed auxin perception locally but did not change auxin responses at the site of primordia initiation.
source: Importantly, inducing HEC1 in stem cells repressed auxin perception locally but did not change auxin responses at the site of primordia initiation, demonstrating that HEC1 controls auxin signalling strictly cell autonomously (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-G.

claim: HEC function regulates cellular sensitivity to cytokinin and auxin signals in a domain-specific manner.
source: Taken together, these results showed that HEC function regulates cellular sensitivity to cytokinin and auxin signals in a domain-specific manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: HEC activity was sufficient to modulate phytohormonal balance in diverse cellular contexts independent of the regulatory environment.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that HEC activity was sufficient to modulate phytohormonal balance in diverse cellular contexts independent of the regulatory environment and underlined its central role in regulating the crosstalk between auxin and cytokinin responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations in both SAM and root meristem.

claim: HEC1 binds to 6930 binding regions in 5250 unique genes with 74.5% of the events located within 3 kb upstream of transcriptional start sites.
source: We found 6930 binding regions of HEC1 in 5250 unique genes with 74.5% of the events located within 3 kb upstream of transcriptional start sites (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The HEC1 DNA binding pattern was distinct from those of other bHLH transcription factors.
source: The HEC1 DNA binding pattern was distinct from those of other bHLH transcription factors, suggesting that our ChIP-seq had indeed captured the chromatin binding universe of HEC1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 957 genes were significantly regulated after three hours of HEC1 induction by dex.
source: We identified 957 significantly regulated genes after three hours of HEC1 induction by dex and 815 transcripts after induction by dex and simultaneous inhibition of protein biosynthesis by cycloheximide (cyc) (p<0.05) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: One of the most highly enriched DNA motif in HEC1 binding regions was a G-Box.
source: Next, we carefully analysed the identified binding regions and in line with the quality of our data-set, one of the most highly enriched DNA motif in HEC1 binding regions was a G-Box, the sequence known to be the preferentially bound by bHLH transcription factors (E-value = 1.4 e-141) (Figure 7B) (Lau et al., 2014; Pfeiffer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7B and citations.

claim: Auxin response elements (ARE) were significantly over-represented under HEC1 peaks.
source: Interestingly, auxin response elements (ARE), the DNA cis-regulatory motifs targeted by ARF transcription factors to regulate auxin dependent gene expression, were also significantly over-represented under HEC1 peaks (ARE, E-value = 5.0 e-61).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claim: HEC1 bound to 23 out of 25 promoters of auxin signalling components known to be active in the SAM.
source: Strikingly, we found that HEC1 bound to 23 out of 25 promoters of auxin signalling components known to be active in the SAM, a rate significantly higher than expected by chance (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: G-boxes and AREs found in HEC1 binding regions were significantly more closely spaced than expected from their relative positions across the whole genome.
source: Consistently, we observed that G-boxes and AREs found in HEC1 binding regions were significantly more closely spaced than expected from their relative positions across the whole genome (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Both Yeast-2-Hybrid and Bimolecular-Fluorescence Complementation assays robustly demonstrated a physical interaction between MP and HEC1, HEC2, or HEC3.
source: Both Yeast-2-Hybrid and Bimolecular-Fluorescence Complementation assays robustly demonstrated a physical interaction between MP and HEC1, HEC2, or HEC3, respectively and thus suggested that HEC factors could act as transcriptional modifiers for ARF activity (Figure 8A–B) (Simonini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A-B and a citation.

claim: HEC1 and HEC2, as well as their key cofactor SPATULA (SPT) were able to physically interact with BRAHMA in Yeast-two-Hybrid assays.
source: In line with these results, HEC1 and HEC2, as well as their key cofactor SPATULA (SPT) were able to physically interact with BRAHMA in Yeast-two-Hybrid assays (Figure 8C) (Efroni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and a citation.

claim: Transcript levels of MP and PID were substantially reduced 14 hr after dex induction of p16:HEC1-linker-GR plants.
source: To test this, we performed RNA-seq on micro-dissected shoot apices 14 hr after dex induction of p16:HEC1-linker-GR plants. In contrast to the set of early targets, we found that transcript levels of essential components for primordia initiation, such as MP itself, but also PID, a kinase required for proper polar localisation of PIN auxin transporters, were substantially reduced in this dataset (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A dramatic decrease in MP-GFP protein accumulation at the boundary zone was observed after HEC1 induction in this domain.
source: In line with this finding, we observed a dramatic decrease in MP-GFP protein accumulation at the boundary zone after HEC1 induction in this domain, demonstrating the relevance of this interaction in the SAM (Figure 8E–F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8E-F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PIN1-GFP polarity was severely disturbed after HEC1 induction.
source: Consistent with the decrease of MP-GFP accumulation and the global collapse of auxin output observed by DR5v2, we found that PIN1-GFP polarity was severely disturbed after HEC1 induction (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Auxin co-treatment rescued MP mRNA expression levels after HEC1 induction.
source: In line with our RNA-seq data, we observed a significant reduction of MP expression 24 hr after HEC1 induction (Figure 9A). However, co-treatment with auxin rescued MP mRNA expression levels, indicating that our approach to stabilize the auxin feedback system was successful (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Auxin co-treatment suppressed the inhibition of primordia initiation caused by pCUC2:HEC1-linker-GR and p16:HEC1-linker-GR inductions.
source: Strikingly, although pCUC2:HEC1-linker-GR and p16:HEC1-linker-GR inductions alone inhibited primordia initiation, auxin co-treatment suppressed this phenotype (Figure 9C–J, Figure 9—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9C-J and Figure 9—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Wild type plants displayed a substantially smaller SAM under low light conditions.
source: In line with previous studies, we observed that wild type plants displayed a substantially smaller SAM under low light conditions (Jones et al., 2017), and additionally observed a three-fold reduction in cytokinin responses compared to plants grown under normal light intensity (Figure 10A,C,E,F,H,J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10A,C,E,F,H,J and a citation.

claim: In contrast to wild type, hec1,2,3 plants did not show significant changes in the size of SAMs under low light.
source: In contrast to wild type, we did not observe significant changes in the size of SAMs in hec1,2,3 plants under low light, demonstrating that HEC genes are required for SAM adaptation to environmental changes (Figure 10B,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10B,D,E.

claim: Even in hec1,2,3, cytokinin signalling was responsive to nutritional status and decreased TCSn reporter activity was observed similar to wild type plants.
source: Interestingly, even in hec1,2,3, cytokinin signalling was responsive to nutritional status and we observed a decreased TCSn reporter activity similar to wild type plants (Figure 10F–J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10F-J.

claim: HEC genes may have a key role during SAM adaptation to environmental challenges.
source: Taken together, this experiment revealed that HEC genes may have a key role during SAM adaptation to environmental challenges and suggested that regulating the timing of cell fate transitions might be important for developmental plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low light experiment data.
